lead: Semen retention is the practice of deliberately avoiding ejaculation, often for weeks or months, and sometimes extended to avoiding masturbation and pornography as in the NoFap movement. In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as a way to gain energy, focus, confidence and attractiveness [1][2].

Versions of the practice appear in Taoist texts on ejaculation control and in the nineteenth-century notion of karezza, and the modern online form grew from the NoFap community founded in 2011 [3][4]. Its testosterone claims trace to a 2003 abstinence study that was retracted in 2021 [4].

Peer-reviewed analyses of social media content found that semen-retention material is widely viewed and often inaccurate, and clinicians have reported a Dhat-like anxiety syndrome in men who follow retention groups [5][6][7].

paras: Chinese texts describe ejaculation-control methods, and Indian traditions have related practices. Alice Stockham coined 'karezza' in the nineteenth century for intercourse without ejaculation [3].

NoFap was founded by Alexander Rhodes in June 2011 after a Reddit thread about a 2003 study reporting a testosterone rise after seven days of abstinence. The paper was retracted in 2021, and the community reported about 1.2 million users by 2025 [4].

Posters on looksmax.org describe retention as increasing motivation, emotional control and workout energy, with one thread titled around the practice being 'real' [2]. Others dispute it; one poster argues that regular ejaculation keeps testosterone high and that retention benefits depend on sexual activity [8].

An analysis of TikTok and Instagram found men's health content, including semen retention, widely viewed and frequently inaccurate [5]. A 2024 paper in the same field reported Dhat syndrome, a culture-bound anxiety about semen loss, emerging in the United States from NoFap-type groups [6], and an earlier study found Dhat-like symptoms among White British men [7]. A review of social media and andrology discusses the retention content as speculation [9].
The therapist Paula Hall has said there is little medical evidence for the claimed changes [4].

Researchers have reported distress linked to relapse-focused framing of abstinence [4]. Retention-adjacent techniques such as ejaculation control are not reliable contraception or infection prevention [3].

No controlled trials of semen retention for appearance were found. Related literature consists of social media content analyses [5][9], a report of Dhat-type syndrome in Western men [6][7], and a review of online ejaculation training programs [10].
